pl-l3d18c1-d1e117.summary: Turns to Christ's merit, on which some say he merited not for himself but only for his members.
claims: Some say Christ merited only for his members.

pl-l3d18c1-d1e120.summary: Answers that he merited for his members redemption from the devil, sin, and penalty, and the opening of the kingdom, the fiery sword removed so entry lies open; but he also merited for himself the glory of impassibility and immortality, as Phil 2:8–9 says: he became obedient unto death, therefore God exalted him and gave him the name above every name. The humility of the passion was the merit of exaltation, and exaltation the reward of humility.
claims: Christ merited redemption for his members.
Christ merited his own exaltation by his humble obedience.

pl-l3d18c1-d1e126.summary: Cites Augustine on Phil 2: to be glorified by resurrection Christ was first humbled by the passion; humility is the merit of glory, glory the reward of humility. All this was in the form of a servant; in the form of God glory always was and will be.
claims: Humility is the merit of glory.
Christ's merit concerns the form of a servant.

pl-l3d18c1-d1e136.summary: Cites Ambrose on the same chapter: here is shown what and how much humility merits.

pl-l3d18c1-d1e145.summary: Concludes that Christ by the humility and obedience of the passion merited the glorification of his body and also the impassibility of his soul: before death his soul was passible and his flesh mortal, but after death, by the merit of humility, his soul was made impassible and his flesh immortal.
claims: Christ merited the glorification of his body and the impassibility of his soul.

pl-l3d18c1-d1e148.summary: Leaves open, as not certain from authority, whether his soul became impassible when his flesh became immortal at the moment of resurrection, or immediately after separation from the flesh.
claims: The timing of the soul's impassibility is uncertain.

pl-l3d18c1.summary: Against those who say Christ merited only for his members, Lombard holds that he merited for his members redemption from the devil, sin, and penalty, and the opening of the kingdom, and for himself the glory of impassibility and immortality: Phil 2:8–9 shows that his humble obedience in the passion merited his exaltation (Augustine, Ambrose). He merited bodily glorification and the impassibility of his soul. Whether the soul became impassible at the moment of resurrection or right after death is not certain from authority.
claims: Christ merited for himself as well as for his members.
Christ merited for his members redemption and the opening of the kingdom.
Christ's humility in the passion merited his exaltation.
Christ merited the impassibility of his soul and the immortality of his flesh.
